newsitem.title: USA: Ill. home-rule powers under attack-county official.
newsitem.headline: Ill. home-rule powers under attack-county official.

text.p: A day after Illinois' largest county dropped plans for a controversial 1,500 percent hike in a real estate transfer tax, a county official warned that the state was out to erode home-rule powers of local governments.

Thomas Glaser, chief financial officer of Cook County, said Tuesday the tax increase proposal was spurred by legislation passed by the Illinois House earlier this month and expected to be approved by the Senate early next month that would require home-rule governments to hold referendums on real estate transfer tax hikes.

The tax increase plan, unveiled by Cook County Board President John Stroger Friday, attracted a groundswell of protests from realtors and others, forcing Stronger late Monday to withdraw the tax increase from consideration at Tuesday's county board meeting.

Glaser said the real focus should not have been on the tax hike, but on the legislature's attempt to reduce home-rule powers. He said the county had no immediate plans to increase the tax, but wanted to retain the option for the future in case the General Assembly passed its bill.

There was also a fear that the loss of the county's power to increase the tax would lead to a rating downgrade. Glaser pointed to recent downgrades of San Diego in the wake of Proposition 218, which California voters approved in November. The measure amended the state Constitution to require voter approval of most tax or fee increases and curtailed the use of many types of assessments.
Glaser said the rating agencies did not express any immediate concern about the county's situation under the legislation.

Still, he pointed out that the bill was just one example of how state lawmakers were stepping on local governments' toes. Others cited by Glaser included a recent law allowing the state to take over a small Chicago airport and unfunded state mandates in the criminal justice area.
"I think at some point the county and the city are going to say enough is enough," Glaser said.

Stroger's proposed real estate transfer tax increase to $7.50 per $1,000 of property value from 50 cents would have netted the county $75 million a year over the $6 million it already collects from the tax.
Glaser said the addition revenues could have been used to help plug a projected $123 million budget shortfall in fiscal 1998, defer debt issuance, fund a self-insurance fund, or for other purposes.

In the wake of the tax hike plan's demise, Glaser said that Stroger plans to lobby Gov. Jim Edgar and state lawmakers for some flexibility with mandated programs. In addition, Glaser said the county may now turn its attention to a possible sales tax increase to bring in more revenues.
